raw_case_text:
A 48-year-old man with no apparent past medical history initially presented with abdominal pain associated with nausea and vomiting. Physical examination was unremarkable. Lab results were significant for anemia, with a hemoglobin level of 11.6 g/dL (14-18), hematocrit 32.2% (42-52), and lipase 164 U/L (13-60). His comprehensive metabolic panel was unrevealing. A CT of the abdomen and pelvis with contrast was performed, which revealed an enlarged pancreas without a focal mass, diffuse surrounding mesenteric edema, mild retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, mild mesenteric lymphadenopathy, rectal wall thickening with perirectal lymphadenopathy, left renal mass measuring 3.7 x 1.4 x 1.4 cm, right renal mass measuring 2.3 x 4.3 x 5.2 cm, marked diffuse urinary bladder wall thickening, and trace pericardial effusion (Figure 1). The concern at the time was for peritoneal carcinomatosis and/or mesenteric tumor. Urology and oncology services were invited to evaluate the patient, both in agreement for a biopsy of the lymph node; in addition, urine cytology and HIV were tested.
Urine cytology revealed atypical lymphocytes. Renal biopsy revealed diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL). Bone marrow biopsy was consistent with involvement of B-cell lymphoma. HTLV-I/II antibody was negative. HIV screening returned with a positive result. Initial CD4 was 440/mul with a percentage of 14%, and HIV RNA viral load by PCR was 61800 copies/mL. Hepatitis C virus screening was negative; hepatitis B screening was positive for the core antibody and surface antibody but negative for surface antigen. His lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) was above the upper limit of the detection for our lab, >2500 U/L (135-225). Cerebrospinal fluid at the time revealed atypical lymphocytes.
Biopsy of the kidney mass revealed atypical lymphocytes positive for CD45, CD20, PAX-5, and CD10, while negative for CD5, CD30, MUM-1, BCL-1 (cyclin D1), BCL-2, BCL-6, c-myc, CD68, CD34, CD117, and MPO, with a high proliferation index (Ki-67) of 80% approximately. The morphology was consistent with diffuse B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), NOS, and germinal center B-cell subtype involving the kidney. A subsequent bone marrow biopsy revealed involvement by DLBCL (Figure 1).
His Revised International Prognostic Indicator (R-IPI) was calculated to be 4, NCCN-IPI of 5, and CNS-IPI of 4. Decision was made to offer him dose-adjusted rituximab, etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin (R-EPOCH) to treat his disease. For HIV, he was treated with raltegravir, tenofovir, and emtricitabine, with a subsequent decrease in viral load to our laboratory's threshold for undetectable. This regimen was chosen specifically for the tenofovir to act as prophylaxis to suppress hepatitis B virus reactivation. In addition, he was treated with fluconazole and acyclovir for antimicrobial prophylaxis. He received 3 cycles of chemotherapy and 1 dose of intrathecal methotrexate, with initial improvement in renal lesions. However, after the third cycle, he presented with dysphagia, Bell's palsy, and diffuse bone pain. Neurology service was consulted recommending MRI of the brain without contrast, which was unremarkable. Subsequent CSF flow cytometry was positive for CD10+ B-cells, with a conclusion of DLBCL infiltrating the CNS. Gastroenterology service was consulted, who performed an EGD but found no explanation for dysphagia. ENT service found mucous in the postcricoid region but had no acute interventions to offer, and evaluation by the speech and language pathologist revealed marked pharyngeal dysphagia, with high risk for aspiration.
A repeat CT of the chest without contrast revealed a right pericardial mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. At that time, he did not report any chest pain, dyspnea, or cough. His vital signs were remarkable only for sinus tachycardia of 110 beats per minute, and he was normotensive, tolerated room air, and maintained good mentation. A subsequent echocardiogram revealed a large loculated pericardial effusion near the right ventricle, with echocardiographic evidence of tamponade. A large mass could be appreciated in the right atrium in the lateral wall, possibly obstructing the IVC. Cardiac mass size was 2.1 cm  x  2.5 cm (Figure 2). This was concerning for disease recurrence. He was transferred to the coronary care unit for monitoring but did not show any clinical signs of cardiac tamponade. Treatment options were discussed with the patient, who opted for palliative care measures and a transfer to hospice care.
The patient's wishes were followed. A PEG tube was placed for nourishment, and his pain was controlled with opioid analgesics. Plans to transfer him to inpatient hospice care were put in place. Unfortunately, the patient expired before he could be discharged, 5 months following initial diagnosis of DLBCL, and within 3 weeks of pericardial involvement being discovered. His dysphagia never resolved and was likely related to the discovered cardiac mass.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 48-year-old male presenting with abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient presented with acute abdominal pain accompanied by nausea and vomiting. Cross-sectional abdominal imaging demonstrated bilateral renal masses, diffuse mesenteric edema, and generalized lymphadenopathy, prompting inpatient oncologic evaluation. After initial clinical response to systemic immunochemotherapy, he developed secondary subacute neurological deterioration characterized by acute dysphagia, facial nerve palsy, and diffuse skeletal pain.
subjective.past_medical_history: No documented prior chronic medical conditions; serologic evidence of past resolved hepatitis B infection (positive anti-HBc and anti-HBs with negative HBsAg).
subjective.review_of_systems: Initial: Abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting. Second admission: Severe dysphagia, facial droop, diffuse bone pain; denies chest pain, shortness of breath, cough, fever, or hematuria.

objective.physical_examination: Initial examination: Abdomen soft without localized tenderness, palpable organomegaly, or palpable mass. Second admission: Sinus tachycardia (110 beats/min), normotensive, room air SpO2 normal, oriented and alert; neurological examination revealed a right-sided peripheral facial nerve (Bell's) palsy and marked pharyngeal dysphagia; cardiopulmonary examination revealed no jugular venous distension, audible murmurs, or clinical signs of tamponade.
objective.routine_investigations: Complete blood count: Hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, hematocrit 32.2%. Biochemical markers: Serum lipase 164 U/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) > 2,500 U/L (reference: 135-225 U/L); comprehensive metabolic panel otherwise within normal limits. Urine cytology: Atypical lymphocytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis: Initial analysis revealed atypical lymphocytes; repeat CSF flow cytometry following neurological progression confirmed clonal CD10+ B-cell infiltration. Infectious serologies: HTLV-I/II antibody negative, HCV antibody negative, HBV core and surface antibodies positive with surface antigen negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Abdomen and pelvis CT: Diffuse pancreatic enlargement without focal mass, extensive mesenteric and retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy, perirectal lymphadenopathy with rectal wall thickening, bilateral renal masses (left renal mass 3.7 x 1.4 x 1.4 cm; right renal mass 2.3 x 4.3 x 5.2 cm), diffuse bladder wall thickening, and trace pericardial effusion. Renal core biopsy: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), germinal center subtype; immunohistochemistry positive for CD45, CD20, PAX-5, and CD10, negative for CD5, CD30, MUM-1, BCL-1, BCL-2, BCL-6, and c-myc, with Ki-67 proliferation index ~80%. Bone marrow biopsy: Concordant infiltration by DLBCL. Brain MRI: Unremarkable without focal parenchymal lesions. Upper endoscopy (EGD): Normal esophagus without mucosal mass. Chest CT (follow-up): Right pericardial mass with mediastinal lymphadenopathy. Transthoracic echocardiogram: Large loculated pericardial effusion adjacent to the right ventricle with echocardiographic evidence of tamponade, and a 2.1 x 2.5 cm right atrial lateral wall mass potentially obstructing the inferior vena cava.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation:
Definitive diagnosis: Newly diagnosed human immunodeficiency virus (HIV-1) infection (CD4 count 440 cells/microL [14%], HIV RNA viral load 61,800 copies/mL) presenting with advanced stage IV Diffuse Large B-Cell Lymphoma (DLBCL, germinal center phenotype; R-IPI 4, NCCN-IPI 5, CNS-IPI 4) with bilateral renal, bone marrow, leptomeningeal CNS, and intracardiac right atrial/pericardial involvement.
Plan & Outcome: Initiated on HAART with raltegravir, tenofovir, and emtricitabine (providing tenofovir for HBV prophylaxis) and opportunistic infection prophylaxis with fluconazole and acyclovir. Received three cycles of dose-adjusted R-EPOCH chemotherapy and intrathecal methotrexate. Following disease progression with CNS leptomeningeal infiltration and cardiac involvement, the patient elected for palliative comfort measures. A percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy (PEG) tube was placed for nutritional support, and pain was controlled with opioids; the patient succumbed to progressive lymphoma five months after diagnosis.
